Consult Summary:
- 50-year-old woman with 5–6 days of persistent dry cough and runny nose, associated with chills, myalgias, fatigue, and sleep disturbance from coughing. No dyspnea with usual activity, no chest pain; brief diarrhea at onset resolved.
- Past history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension on metformin and lisinopril. Clinical impression: self-limiting viral upper respiratory illness. Supportive care advised; return if no improvement or worsening.

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Acute viral upper respiratory illness with dry cough (onset ~5–6 days ago).
- Symptoms: continuous dry cough (worse at night), rhinorrhea, chills/shivering, generalized myalgias (arms/legs), lethargy/weakness, sore throat from coughing only, transient diarrhea at onset (resolved), generally tired.
- Pertinent negatives: no productive sputum, no chest pain, no baseline breathlessness with walking (only during coughing bouts), no ear pain/blockage/discharge, no nausea/vomiting, appetite OK, normal urination, no rash.
- Social: lives with partner (well); working in IT; took 1 day off but has been attending work.
- Exam: no in-person exam or vitals recorded (telephone consult).
- Impression: Viral upper respiratory tract infection. Expected course 7–10 days.
- Management discussed: rest, maintain hydration, regular paracetamol (acetaminophen) as needed; consider 1–2 days off work due to cough/infectivity; safety net—return if not improving in 2–3 days, if fever persists, if breathing worsens; possible consideration of antibiotics if still febrile and cough not improving at review.

Issue 2:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Status: patient reports regular follow-up and controlled since starting medication.
- Medication: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Counseling intersecting with alcohol intake provided.

Issue 3:
- Hypertension.
- Status: patient reports controlled on medication with regular checks.
- Medication: Lisinopril (dose/route/frequency not documented). Note: clinician verbalized “Zinopril” during consult—conflict noted.

Issue 4:
- Alcohol use.
- Intake: wine ~2–3 glasses on up to three evenings per week; rarely intoxicated.
- Counseling: advised to reduce—suggested cut down to two glasses per week for a few weeks, then further reduce and consider cessation, particularly given hypertension/diabetes.

Medications:
- Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Lisinopril (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- No known drug allergies.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Hypertension.
- Family history: father with type 2 diabetes.

Social History:
- Lives with partner; partner currently well.
- Occupation: IT developer.
- Tobacco: former smoker; quit ~6 months ago.
- Alcohol: wine, ~2–3 glasses up to three evenings/week.

Preventative History:
- Not discussed: cervical screening test, mammogram, prostate blood test (not applicable), fecal occult blood test, bone mineral density, vaccinations, optometry review, skin check.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: not recorded.
- Examination: none performed (telephone consult). Patient intermittently coughing during call.

Plan:
- Supportive care for viral URI: rest, fluids, paracetamol (acetaminophen) as needed.
- Work: consider 1–2 days off for rest and to reduce transmission risk; reassess ability to return early next week.
- Follow-up: return in 2–3 days if no improvement; sooner if breathing worsens, persistent fever, or symptoms escalate. Possible evaluation for antibiotics if still febrile and cough not improving at review.
- Lifestyle: reduce alcohol intake as discussed, particularly in context of T2DM and hypertension.
- Usual chronic disease follow-up to continue with regular provider.

Quality checks:
● Missing/expected elements: no vitals; no physical exam; no COVID/flu testing discussed; medication doses/routes/frequencies not documented; vaccination and screening history not discussed; no current blood glucose/BP readings reviewed.
● Internal conflicts: patient states lisinopril; clinician repeated “Zinopril” (conflict noted).
● Transcript quality: generally clear; minor pauses and overlaps; telephone format limits examination.
